transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-06-24
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood Infra), Evelyn (CTO SentinelEdge), Markus (Lead ML Eng), Priya (SRE), Anita (Security)

Auto-summary: quick rundown on KV cache design, eviction heuristics, paging behavior when context exceeds local KV capacity, and prefix reuse pathologies. Action items captured.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda \u0003 we want to walk through how our KV cache works, show eviction / paging patterns, and then look at your long-context models.
[00:28] Evelyn: Good, yeah we saw some latency spikes in prod when conversations hit ~30k tokens, so hoping to understand root cause.
[01:02] Liam: cool. high level: our KV cache is shard-local per GPU, we keep per-seq KV with LRU-ish eviction but with heuristics for prefix reuse to avoid thrashing. when the working set exceeds GPU memory we page to a host-backed slab, which adds tail latency.
[01:45] Markus: when you say paging, is that host RAM, NVMe, or do you do streaming across network to another server?
[02:10] Diego: primarily host RAM + optional NVMe spill. we avoid remote network pages for latency reasons; if customers use private deployments they can opt into NVMe spilling for very long contexts.
[02:35] Anita: quick sec \u0003 on private deployments, what's encrypted at rest? is spilled KV encrypted with KMS?
[02:50] Maya: yes, spills are encrypted using customer KMS when in Private mode; we'll attach the security pack.
[03:12] [Speaker crosstalk] Priya: so the spikes we saw \u0003 they were concurrent with heavy prompting and many active sessions, not a single long session. could contention be a factor?
[03:45] Liam: absolutely. two orthogonal things: per-session long-context causing large KV per session, and multi-tenancy causing aggregate working set growth. batching also plays a role because batched requests bring in more KV into active working set.
[04:20] Markus: can you explain prefix reuse heuristics? we suspect our conversations reuse a lot of similar system prompts and we see evictions of those primes.
[04:47] Liam: sure. prefix reuse: if multiple sessions share identical prefixes we maintain a shared reference to the cached KV for that prefix. eviction policy weights share-factor higher, so heavily-shared prefixes are evicted less aggressively. but when small variations to the prefix exist (even punctuation), that sharing breaks and you see lots of near-duplicate cache entries.
[05:30] Evelyn: aha \u0003 so canonicalization of prompts would help?
[05:38] Liam: yes, normalizing templates reduces duplication. we can also enable prefix fingerprinting to do fuzzy matches, but that increases CPU overhead during lookups. tradeoff.
[06:10] Diego: something we saw in some customer tests \u0003 quantized models use smaller KV representations which reduces memory pressure but sometimes increases compute per token and can change eviction cadence.
[06:36] Markus: are you seeing quantization affecting correctness for our retrieval-augmented prompts?
[06:50] Liam: mostly fine for 8-bit quantization on typical chat models; for some retrieval-heavy workloads small numeric differences can affect logit ordering, so we recommend an eval sweep.
[07:20] Priya: what tuning knobs are available? we are particularly sensitive to tail latency (95/99).
[07:36] Liam: knobs: per-gpu cache size, eviction aggressiveness, shared-prefix threshold, host-spill threshold, and batching window. you can trade cost for latency by enlarging cache or reducing batch windows.
[08:00] Maya: and besides config, we have routing/fallback \u0003 you can route latency sensitive sessions to reserved Dedicated pool with higher memory GPUs.
[08:22] Evelyn: what about metrics we should collect to debug?
[08:28] Diego: key metrics: KV hit ratio, avg KV size per session, eviction rate, host-spill rate, paging latency, per-token compute time, and batch composition (tokens per batch). we'll send sample dashboards.
[09:05] [02 minute break in call noted]
[11:10] Markus: we saw eviction spikes around 30k tokens, and paging latencies shot up to ~450ms on some requests \u0003 is that consistent with host-RAM spill?
[11:35] Liam: yes 400-600ms is plausible for host spill in high-contention scenarios; NVMe spill can be seconds unless async prefetching is used.
[12:02] Markus: what about incremental KV eviction vs chunked eviction? we saw bursts where many entries were evicted at once.
[12:18] Diego: our eviction runs periodically to reclaim contiguous blocks; in memory-pressure spikes you get batch eviction which causes a transient cache miss storm. smoothing the eviction window reduces that at the cost of higher steady memory overhead.
[12:50] Evelyn: is there a recommended approach for long-lived sessions (e.g., long documents or multi-hour conversations)?
[13:05] Liam: options: 1) store older prefixes in long-term persistent cache and only keep hot prefixes in GPU cache (requires async prefetch), 2) chunk long contexts and summarize/condense older history to reduce KV size, 3) use model-level windowing and archive earlier context as embeddings. each has tradeoffs for latency and freshness.
[13:55] Markus: curious about option 1 \u0003 async prefetch seems to add complexity; do you support background prefetch on Dedicated?
[14:10] Diego: yes, Dedicated and Private can enable prefetch threads that pull required KV blocks from NVMe into host RAM prior to GPU execution, reducing tail latency. we'll include config examples.
[14:45] Priya: during our incidents we saw significant prefix reuse mismatch caused by small differences in user metadata included in prompt. any suggestions?
[15:02] Liam: sanitize or template out user-specific fields, or use a hashing layer that strips low-entropy tokens before fingerprinting. we also support canonicalization hooks at the SDK level.
[15:35] Evelyn: you mentioned batch size effects earlier \u0003 I want details: we batch to maximize throughput but need to keep sub-200ms p95 for some endpoints.
[15:52] Liam: batching window controls; smaller windows = lower latency but lower throughput efficiency. also prefix reuse across batch improves cache hit ratio because one batch can leverage shared KV. tradeoff matrix: latency targets vs cost. we can run microbenchmarks to show curves.
[16:25] Markus: could you run a microbenchmark with our model + prompts and show hit ratio and p95/p99 at 50/200/500 concurrent sessions?
[16:40] Maya: yes, that's part of the proposed pilot. we'll run a 3x sweep and share a spreadsheet.
[17:00] Anita: on compliance, when you page to NVMe in Private mode is the NVMe disk inside customer's VPC? who controls keys?
[17:18] Maya: in Private deployment, NVMe is in the customer's environment; KMS keys are customer-managed; logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. we'll attach security architecture and SOC2 docs.
[17:45] Markus: about prefix sharing, can you show a diagram of the shared-prefix refcounts and how eviction respects reuse?
[17:58] Liam: yep, I'll draw that out \u0003 essentially an entry has a refcount of active sessions; eviction score = recency * size / (1 + refcountFactor). the refcountFactor biases towards keeping shared prefixes. it's heuristic-based and tunable.
[18:30] Evelyn: we intermittently saw identical prefixes still evicted \u0003 could be an implementation bug or fingerprinting mismatch.
[18:45] Liam: possible; need to check canonicalization + fingerprint thresholds. if your prompts have whitespace or minor tokens, fingerprints differ. we should look at exact examples from logs.
[19:10] Priya: we'll provide a sample of 10 sessions with tokens and timestamps.
[19:25] Maya: great. Diego, can you explain how quantization changes KV memory layout?
[19:35] Diego: quantized KV reduces per-token bytes by ~2-4x depending on quant scheme. that reduces eviction pressure but shifts cost to more compute during dequantization or attention kernels. it can also reduce the effectiveness of prefix sharing if quantization is lossy in ways that change equality checks; we use fingerprints pre-quantization.
[20:10] Markus: do you have recommended GPU types for large KV workloads?
[20:18] Liam: GPUs with larger device memory (A100 80GB, H100) reduce spill frequency. for Dedicated we recommend partitioned pools: some nodes optimized for latency (bigger memory, less concurrency), others optimized for throughput (smaller memory, larger batch sizes).
[20:50] Evelyn: any quick wins to reduce our tail latency before we do a pilot?
[20:58] Liam: yes: template canonicalization, increase per-GPU cache limit for critical routes, reduce batching window on latency-sensitive endpoints, adjust eviction smoothing.
[21:30] Priya: can Redwood run an experiment where we throttle concurrency to see impact on eviction rate?
[21:40] Maya: yes we'll coordinate timing \u0003 that's part of the staging experiment.
[22:05] Markus: you mentioned mixed-precision and quantization \u0003 does Redwood automatic kernel selection change for quantized models?
[22:18] Diego: yes, runtime chooses kernels; quantized paths sometimes use specialized kernels which change per-token compute time, we can show per-kernel timings.
[22:55] [Short screen-share: Liam shows KV-cache heatmap visual]
[24:10] Liam: here you can see hot prefixes with high refcount; eviction occurs in the blue areas where working set exceeds cache. note the vertical stripes \u0003 those are batch pulls bringing in new tokens simultaneously.
[24:45] Evelyn: I see the correlation between batch spikes and eviction storms.
[25:00] Lily (typo in auto speaker): sorry \u0003 that's me interjecting, ignore
[25:15] Markus: is there an API to pin a prefix in cache? for VIP sessions we want to pin system prompts.
[25:28] Liam: yes, we support pinning at session creation in Dedicated/Private, with TTL and refcount semantics. pinning prevents eviction unless explicitly unpinned or memory pressure is catastrophic.
[25:55] Priya: awesome. about instrumentation, can we get per-session KV metrics exported to Prometheus?
[26:08] Diego: we emit per-route and per-server metrics; per-session is more expensive but we can emit sampled traces or push to your aggregator via webhook.
[26:30] Anita: security concern \u0003 do any of these cached KVs contain PII? we need controls to scrub sensitive tokens before caching.
[26:45] Liam: caching is opt-in per-route; you can disable caching for routes that include PII, or enable token-redaction hooks to scrub sensitive tokens prior to cache entry creation.
[27:10] Evelyn: okay we will prepare a list of routes with PII and those without.
[27:30] Markus: on the microbenchmark, can you also measure memory fragmentation effects and after-long-uptime steady-state behavior? we saw fragmentation after 48 hours.
[27:46] Diego: yes fragmentation is real when you have many variable-sized entries. our GC compactor runs during low-load windows; we can show compaction-less and compaction-on traces.
[28:20] Maya: let's quickly go over the proposed pilot: 1) Redwood runs benchmark on our staging model with your prompts, 2) run eviction/paging test during 2-hour window, 3) iterate on tuning (prefix canonicalization, cache sizes), 4) evaluate p95/p99 and cost delta.
[28:50] Evelyn: timeline?
[28:56] Maya: target start 2026-06-29, planning call 2026-06-30.
[29:12] Priya: for the first run, we'll allocate a staging cluster with similar concurrency patterns. Markus will handle.
[29:25] Markus: yes will provision.
[29:40] Liam: one more note \u0003 when multiple models share the same GPU pool, cross-model eviction can happen; consider model pinning or separate pools for large-view models.
[30:00] Evelyn: do you have any documented best-practices for summarizing long history instead of keeping raw tokens?
[30:12] Liam: yes we have a summarization pattern and libraries for condensing history into short context + retrieval embeddings. we'll share a doc.
[30:35] [Customer asks about billing impacts]
[30:45] Maya: additional memory or Dedicated nodes increase cost; we will provide a cost vs latency table in the benchmark sheet.
[31:05] Anita: also need architecture diagram for security review \u0003 please include network flows and KMS details.
[31:18] Maya: noted.
[31:30] Evelyn: any final clarifications?
[31:40] Priya: can you capture exact sample log lines where eviction was triggered? that will help correlate metrics.
[31:50] Liam: yes we'll pull those traces and include them in the sheet.
[32:05] Maya: recap of action items and owners \u0003 we'll send notes and materials by EOD tomorrow.
[32:20] Evelyn: thanks all, this was useful.
[32:30] [Meeting ends around 15:55 UTC]
